summary: The BGP Monitoring Protocol is used to monitor BGP sessions and provide a convenient interface for obtaining route views, replacing earlier screen scraping. This standards-track RFC aims to keep BMP simple, useful and easy to implement. It is not a routing protocol.

eli5.summary: A window into what a router has learned about the Internet's routes, so you do not have to read it off its screen.

subtitle: A one-way feed from a router to a monitoring station, replacing screen scraping for BGP route views.

tldr.problem: Researchers and operators want to see the contents of a router's BGP routing tables and the updates it receives, but standard protocol mechanisms cannot provide that. Before BMP, screen scraping was the usual approach.
tldr.mechanism: The router opens a TCP session to a monitoring station and sends it a stream of BMP messages: an initial dump of each peer's Adj-RIB-In, then incremental updates, peer up and down events and optional statistics. The station never sends anything back.
tldr.outcome: BMP gives a convenient, simple interface for route views, but it is not a routing protocol. RFC 7854 is a Proposed Standard and has since been updated by RFC 8671, RFC 9069, RFC 9515 and RFC 9736.

today: RFC 7854 is a Proposed Standard and has not been obsoleted, but it has been updated by RFC 8671, RFC 9069, RFC 9515 and RFC 9736, so read it together with those updates.

sections.title: Why BMP Exists
sections.content:
Many researchers and network operators want access to the contents of a router's BGP Routing Information Bases (RIBs), plus a view of the protocol updates the router is receiving. The RFC says this monitoring task cannot be done with standard protocol mechanisms, so before BMP the data could only be obtained through screen scraping.

The BGP Monitoring Protocol (BMP) provides ongoing access to the Adj-RIB-In of each peer, plus a periodic dump of certain statistics. From a high level, BMP can be thought of as the messages received on the various monitored BGP sessions multiplexed together. The design goals are to keep it simple, useful, easily implemented and minimally service affecting. It is explicitly not suitable for use as a routing protocol.

Two terms matter throughout. The Adj-RIB-In is the unprocessed routing information advertised to the router by a peer, also called the pre-policy Adj-RIB-In here. The post-policy Adj-RIB-In is what remains after inbound policy has been applied, but before route selection forms the Loc-RIB.
sections.eli5: Before BMP, people had to read a router's screen to learn what routes it knew. BMP lets the router send that information straight to a computer instead.

sections.title: Sessions and Their Lifecycle
sections.content:
BMP runs over TCP, and every option is set by configuration on the monitored router. No BMP message is ever sent from the monitoring station to the router. The router may take steps to stop the station sending data, such as half-closing the TCP session or setting the window size to 0, or it may silently discard anything the station sends. One of the two parties is configured as the active side that connects, and the other listens passively. If the active side cannot connect, it retries with some form of backoff; the RFC suggests exponential backoff with an initial 30 seconds and a maximum of 720 seconds.

The router may restrict the IP addresses it will accept connections from. It SHOULD limit simultaneous connections per address, with a default of 1, and it MUST limit the rate at which sessions are established; a suggested default is 2 sessions per minute. There is no handshake: messages simply start flowing once the TCP connection is up.

A session starts with an Initiation message (the router MUST begin with it), followed by a Peer Up message for each monitored BGP peer in the Established state, then that peer's routes as Route Monitoring messages. After the last route for a peer the router MUST send an End-of-RIB message for it. Afterwards it sends incremental updates, and possibly Stats Reports or new Initiation messages. The session ends when the TCP session closes for any reason; the router MAY send a Termination message first. If the station wants to stop or restart, it simply drops the connection.
sections.eli5: The router phones the note-taker, introduces itself, tells them who it is talking to, reads out everything it knows, and then keeps whispering updates. The note-taker only listens.

sections.title: The BMP Headers
sections.content:
Every BMP message starts with a common header: a 1-byte Version, a 4-byte Message Length (covering headers, data and any encapsulated messages) and a 1-byte Message Type. The version is 3 for everything in this specification; versions 1 and 2 were used by draft versions, and version 0 is reserved and MUST NOT be sent. A receiver MUST ignore message types it does not recognize.

Most messages then carry a per-peer header describing which BGP peer the data came from. It holds the Peer Type, Peer Flags, an 8-byte Peer Distinguisher, a Peer Address (16 bytes, with IPv4 addresses placed in the last 4 and the rest zero-filled), the Peer AS, the Peer BGP ID and a timestamp in seconds and microseconds since January 1, 1970 UTC. A timestamp of zero means the time is unavailable.

Three peer types exist: 0 Global Instance Peer, 1 RD Instance Peer and 2 Local Instance Peer. Together with the Peer Distinguisher, they tell apart peers whose addresses might overlap, for example in Layer 3 VPNs. The flags byte defines three bits. V says the peer address is IPv6. L says the data is the post-policy Adj-RIB-In (locally sourced routes also carry L=1). A says the legacy 2-byte AS_PATH format is used. The remaining bits MUST be sent as 0 and ignored on receipt.
sections.eli5: Each message starts with a label saying what kind of message it is and how long it is. Many also carry a second label saying which neighbor the news came from.

sections.title: The Seven Message Types
sections.content:
BMP defines seven message types, numbered 0 to 6.

  • Route Monitoring carries a BGP Update PDU after the headers. It gives the initial dump of routes and then ongoing changes.
  • Stats Reports carry a 4-byte count followed by counters and gauges, each as a type, length and data.
  • Peer Down Notification says a peering session ended and why, using reason codes 1 to 5. It implicitly withdraws all routes from that peer, so an implementation MAY omit explicit withdraws.
  • Peer Up Notification says a session reached Established. It includes the local address, local and remote ports, and the full OPEN messages sent and received.
  • Initiation tells the station about the router. The sysDescr and sysName TLVs MUST be sent, and a free-form string TLV may be repeated.
  • Termination says why the router is closing the session. Its Reason TLV is REQUIRED, with codes 0 to 4. After sending it, the router MUST close the TCP session, and the station MUST close it too.
  • Route Mirroring carries verbatim copies of received BGP messages, along with information codes.
sections.eli5: There are seven kinds of note: here are routes, here are some counts, a neighbor left, a neighbor arrived, hello I am this router, goodbye, and an exact photocopy of a message.

sections.title: Route Monitoring and Mirroring
sections.content:
After the session is up, Route Monitoring messages give a snapshot of each peer's Adj-RIB-In using standard BGP Update messages, with no requirement on ordering. A router may send pre-policy routes, post-policy routes or both; the L flag tells them apart, and a withdraw MUST carry the same L flag as the announcement it corresponds to. If the router can say when routes were received it MAY fill in the timestamp; otherwise the timestamp MUST be 0.

Route Monitoring messages are not replicas of what was received. If a prefix changes again before the router gets around to reporting it, the router may report only the final state. This is called state compression, and the PDU sent may differ from the one received, for example because implementations format path attributes differently. The initial dump and incremental updates can run at the same time, so the station must be ready to correlate a withdraw with a route it has already seen; it may also see a bogus withdraw it can safely ignore.

Route Mirroring exists for two reasons. One is a full-fidelity view of every message with no state compression, but the RFC warns this could need unbounded storage, that it is unlikely to suit conventional routers, and that its use is NOT RECOMMENDED unless implementors have weighed the trade-offs. The other is error reporting: when revised error handling for BGP updates (RFC 7606) is in use, errored messages MAY be mirrored with an Errored PDU code, and a Messages Lost code SHOULD be sent if buffer space runs out.
sections.eli5: The router gives a summary of the latest news, not a copy of every letter. If it wants an exact photocopy of every letter, it has to keep a huge pile of paper, so that is discouraged.

sections.title: Statistics, Instances and Local Routes
sections.content:
Stats Reports are optional, but if one is sent it MUST carry at least one statistic. The RFC does not set when to send them, only that timer or threshold settings should be configurable. Counters are 32-bit and gauges are 64-bit. The fourteen defined types, numbered 0 to 13, include prefixes rejected by inbound policy, duplicate advertisements and withdraws, updates invalidated by loops (CLUSTER_LIST, AS_PATH, ORIGINATOR_ID, AS_CONFED), the number of routes in Adj-RIBs-In and in the Loc-RIB, and treat-as-withdraw counts. A receiver MUST ignore unrecognized stat types.

BMP relates to a single BGP instance, so a router with several BGP instances should have several BMP instances, and they SHOULD send distinguishable Initiation messages, for example with different sysNames.

Locally originated routes can be modeled as sent by the router to itself, with its own address in the Peer Address field. In that case no transport session exists, so the Local and Remote Port fields of the Peer Up message MUST be 0.
sections.eli5: The router can also send little report cards with counts, such as how many routes it threw away. If a router runs several routing programs, each one gets its own mailbox.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
BMP gives an outside party a full dump or continuous view of a BGP speaker's routes, which could reveal information not otherwise obtainable. BGP is used in private contexts too, such as L3VPNs. A clever attacker might even infer a router's import policy by comparing the pre-policy routes exposed by BMP with the post-policy routes exported in BGP.

Implementations SHOULD require manual configuration of the monitored and monitoring devices. BMP itself provides no authentication or confidentiality. Without a transport offering mutual authentication, an attacker could pose as the router and feed the station false information, or pose as a station and read BMP data. Without confidentiality, an attacker could read or tamper with data in flight. Where this matters, the RFC says to use IPsec in tunnel mode with pre-shared keys.
sections.eli5: The note-taker sees everything the router knows, so you only want trusted people to listen, and you should keep the phone line private.
